# Modern mode: `;#pragma` lines

Status: design, for 2.0. Nothing of this is implemented yet. Scope (the main file decides), the meaning of `modern` (always the
newest set), the `;#` prefix, the placement and C-like warning pragmas are decided; the other open questions at the end need an answer from Xaymar before the
implementation PRs start.

## Why

BlitzLLVM already has two switches that change how a program behaves compared to the original:

| CLI option | What it changes | Added in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--sane-evaluation-order` | Arguments, operands, array indices and stores are evaluated from left to right, not in the register order of the original (`F(a(), b(), c())` calls `b`, `c`, `a`). | `compiler_order.cpp` |
| `--field-defaults` | `New` sets a field to its default value (`Field lives% = 3`), which the original accepts and never uses. | [#699](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/pull/699) |

Both are options of `blitzcc`, so they live in a build script, a project file of an IDE or the head of the person who
builds the program. The source doesn't say which behaviour it was written for. A program that needs left to right order
silently gives other results when someone builds it without the option, and a library can't ask for the behaviour it
was written against at all.

JavaScript solved the same problem with `"use strict";`: a line at the top of a file that old engines read as a string
that does nothing, and new engines read as a switch. BlitzBasic has no string statement that does nothing, but it has
comments, and every Blitz compiler ignores them.

## Syntax

```blitzbasic
;#pragma modern
```

* A pragma line is a comment that starts with `;#pragma`, directly, with no space between `;` and `#pragma`. The
  original Blitz3D, BlitzPlus, IDEal and every other tool read it as a comment.
* `;#` is the prefix of every compiler directive of BlitzLLVM, `pragma` is the first one. A comment counts as a
  directive only when a known directive word follows `;#` (`;#pragma`, and later ones such as a possible `;#if`), so
  comments like `;#1`, `;#Region` or `;####` stay comments and don't warn.
* After `#pragma` come one or more names, separated by spaces or commas: `;#pragma sane-evaluation-order field-defaults`.
* A name with `no-` in front turns that feature off again: `;#pragma modern no-field-defaults`. Names are read from left
  to right, the last one for a feature wins.
* Names are not case sensitive, like everything else in BlitzBasic.
* Everything after a second `;` on the line is a comment: `;#pragma modern ; written for BlitzLLVM 2.0`.

Why `;#`:

* `;~` is taken: IDEal writes `;~IDEal Editor Parameters:` and `;~F#...` lines at the end of every file it saves.
* `;#pragma` reads like a C or C++ directive, which is what it is, and the prefix leaves room for later directives that
  affect compiling. `;@pragma` was the other candidate (Xaymar: either is fine); `;#` won because it is what people
  coming from C expect.

### Where it may be

Feature pragmas (`modern`, `field-defaults`, ...) only in the comments at the top of a file, before its first statement.
Warning pragmas anywhere, see *Warnings*. Empty lines and other comments may come before
it, which is needed anyway: the pre-commit hook of this repository puts a copyright header in front of every `.bb`
file, and many programs start with a comment that says what they are.

```blitzbasic
; AUTOGENERATED COPYRIGHT HEADER START
; Copyright (C) 2026 Narta Xaymar Dirks
; AUTOGENERATED COPYRIGHT HEADER END
; Space shooter, main file.
;#pragma modern

Graphics 800, 600, 0, 2
```

A feature pragma after the first statement does nothing, and the new warning `pragma-misplaced` (level 1, on by
default) says so. A behaviour that changes in the middle of a file would be hard to read and harder to get right in the
compiler (a Type declared above the line and used below it).

### Unknown names

An unknown name is the warning `pragma-unknown` (level 1), not an error, and the rest of the line still counts. That
way a program written for a newer BlitzLLVM, with a pragma an older one doesn't know yet, still builds on the older one
(with the behaviour of the original for that feature), and a typo gets pointed out. `-Werror=pragma-unknown` makes it an
error for those who prefer that.

## The names

Every feature that a pragma can switch has a CLI option of the same name, and every such CLI option has a pragma. That
keeps the two in step and means the help only has to explain each feature once.

| Pragma | CLI option | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sane-evaluation-order` | `--sane-evaluation-order` | Left to right evaluation, see [Language Quirks](../tools/wiki/pages/Language-Quirks.md#order-of-evaluation). |
| `field-defaults` | `--field-defaults` | `New` applies field defaults, see [Language Quirks](../tools/wiki/pages/Language-Quirks.md#default-values-of-fields). |
| `modern` | `--modern` (new) | All of the above. |

`modern` is the umbrella and always means the newest set (Xaymar, 26 Nov 2026): it turns on every feature that is in
the modern set of the BlitzLLVM it is built with. A feature that joins the set later (see *Later candidates*) is also
turned on by `modern` from then on, and there are no editions such as `modern 2.0`. A program that must not change on an
update lists the single features it wants instead of `modern`, or turns off the ones it doesn't want
(`;#pragma modern no-short-circuit`).

The `no-` forms are only useful together with `modern` or with a CLI option, as every feature is off unless something
turns it on.

### Warnings

Warning pragmas follow C and C++ (`#pragma warning(...)` of MSVC, `#pragma GCC diagnostic` of GCC and clang): they can
be anywhere in a file and apply from their line on, so a single block can be silenced. Two spellings are accepted, the
`-W` options of `blitzcc` without the leading `-`, and the C form:

| Pragma | Same as | What it does from this line on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `W0` .. `W4` | `-W0` .. `-W4` | Warning level. |
| `W<name>`, `warning(enable: <name>)` | `-W<name>` | Turn one warning on, whatever the level is. |
| `Wno-<name>`, `warning(disable: <name>)` | `-Wno-<name>` | Turn one warning off. |
| `Werror` | `-Werror` | Every warning is an error. |
| `Werror=<name>`, `warning(error: <name>)` | `-Werror=<name>` | Make one warning an error. |
| `Werror=<name>`, `error(enable: <name>)` | `-Werror=<name>` | Make one warning an error (same as the row above). |
| `Wno-error=<name>`, `error(disable: <name>)` | `-Wno-error=<name>` | Make one warning a warning again. |
| `warning(push)`, `warning(pop)` | | Save the warning settings, and go back to the saved ones. |
| `error(push)`, `error(pop)` | | The same, for which warnings are errors. |

```blitzbasic
;#pragma modern Wno-implicit-lossy-real-to-int

;#pragma warning(push)
;#pragma warning(disable: field-default-ignored)
Type Legacy
	Field lives% = 3
End Type
;#pragma warning(pop)
```

`warning(...)` and `error(...)` can list several names, separated by spaces or commas. Warnings only have names today;
if they get numbers later, a number works wherever a name does. `warning(push)` and `error(push)` save all warning
settings on the same stack, so either `pop` goes back to the last `push` of either kind. A `pop` without a `push` is the new warning
`pragma-pop-unmatched` (level 1) and does nothing; a `push` that is never popped is fine.

A warning belongs to the file and line of the place it points at (the line and column it reports). Unlike the feature
pragmas, warning settings carry through `Include` like in C (Xaymar, 26 Nov 2026): the program is read as one stream
of lines in the order the compiler reads it, an `Include`d file starts with the warning settings in force at the
`Include` line, and what it changes stays changed after it. A library that wants to keep its own settings to itself
wraps them in `push`/`pop`, as C headers do:

```blitzbasic
; main.bb
;#pragma warning(push)
;#pragma warning(disable: field-default-ignored)
Include "oldlib.bb"     ; Its field defaults don't warn.
;#pragma warning(pop)
Include "newlib.bb"     ; Back to the settings of the build.
```

The pragmas come first, then the `-W` options of the build, then the default level (`-W2`). A file that writes `Wno-error=...` can therefore
escape a `-Werror` of the build for that warning; that is on purpose, as a library knows which of its warnings are
harmless, and it only works for the warning it names.

`pragma-unknown` also covers unknown warning names, so a warning that a newer BlitzLLVM added doesn't break an older one.

### Later candidates

Not part of this design, only listed to check that the scheme has room for them. Each would get its own design first.

* `short-circuit`: `And` and `Or` stop as soon as the result is known, like `AndAlso`/`OrElse` elsewhere. The original
  always evaluates both sides, and they are bitwise.
* `strict`: a variable must be declared (`Local`, `Global`, `Dim`) before it is used, like `Strict` in BlitzMax. A typo
  in a variable name is then an error instead of a new variable that is 0.
* Anything else where the original does something surprising that a program can't rely on in a useful way.

Features that only add something (new commands, `In`/`Out` parameters, `Int32` types) don't need a pragma: a program
that uses them can't be built by the original anyway.

## Scope: the main file decides

Feature pragmas apply to the whole program, and the main file (the one given to `blitzcc`) decides (Xaymar,
26 Nov 2026). There is one behaviour per program, so nobody has to know which file decides what: a Type declared in
`a.bb` and used in `b.bb` behaves like everything else in the program.

An `Include`d file can carry feature pragmas as well, but there they don't switch anything. They say what the file was
written for, and the compiler compares that with the program. A feature an included file asks for differently than the
program uses is the new warning `pragma-mismatch` (level 1), once per file and feature:

```blitzbasic
; main.bb
;#pragma modern
Include "oldlib.bb"     ; No pragma: says nothing, no warning.
Include "newlib.bb"     ; ;#pragma modern: matches, no warning.
Include "strictold.bb"  ; ;#pragma no-sane-evaluation-order: warns.
```

```text
strictold.bb:1:11: warning: 'strictold.bb' was written for the evaluation order of the original, but the program uses
left to right order (;#pragma modern in main.bb). [pragma-mismatch]
```

`-Werror=pragma-mismatch` makes it an error, for programs that would rather not build with a library in the wrong mode.
An included file without a feature pragma says nothing, so the libraries that exist today never warn.

`modern` in an included file stands for every feature of the modern set, so a modern library in a program that turned
one feature off with `no-` warns for that feature only.

Warning pragmas are different: they are positional and carry through `Include` like in C, see *Warnings*.

The shipped includes (`Include "<keys.bb>"` and the others, see [Include files](Include-Files.md)) only hold `Const`s
today, so no feature changes anything in them and they carry no feature pragma. Once one ships functions, it should be
written so that it works in both modes, and then needs no feature pragma either.

Per file scope was the first choice (each file keeps its own behaviour, with a rule per feature for which file decides,
such as "field defaults follow the file of the Type"). It was dropped because users would have to learn those rules
and would guess them wrong: a Type of a modern file used from an old file could reasonably be expected to behave either
way.

## Pragmas and CLI options

Every feature has three levels for the program, and the first one that says something wins:

1. A pragma in the main file (`;#pragma field-defaults` or `;#pragma no-field-defaults`).
2. A CLI option (`--field-defaults`, `--modern`, or a `--no-` form, see below).
3. The behaviour of the original.

So the CLI options keep working as they do today for a main file that says nothing, and `--modern` is the same for all
features at once. A main file with a pragma always behaves the same, whatever the build script says, which is the point
of putting it into the source. The warnings follow the same order (pragmas, then `-W` options, then `-W2`), with the
positional rules of *Warnings*.

New CLI options:

* `--modern`: like `;#pragma modern` in a main file that has no pragma for a feature.
* `--no-<feature>` for every feature (`--no-field-defaults`), to switch one off after `--modern`.

`pragma-mismatch` compares included files with the setting the program ends up with, whichever level it came from.

There is deliberately no option that overrides the pragmas of the main file. For comparing a program against the
original, `blitzcc --ignore-pragmas` could be added later if it is needed (open question 4).

## What else needs to know

* **blitz-lsp**: reads the pragmas like the compiler does (it needs to know which file is the main file of the
  program for that, for example from a setting of the workspace), so the hover text and warnings such as
  `field-default-ignored` match what the compiler will do. Completion offers the known names after `;#pragma`.
* **blitz-format**: leaves pragma lines alone (they are comments). It must not move a comment block that holds one below
  the first statement.
* **blitz-tidy**: a rule could later suggest `;#pragma sane-evaluation-order` for files that call functions with side
  effects in several arguments of one call. Not part of this design.
* **Original Blitz3D and BlitzPlus**: nothing to do, the line is a comment. A program that depends on a pragma gives
  other results there, which is the same situation as with the CLI options today, only now the source says so.
* **Wiki**: a new page `Modern-Mode` (user facing), linked from Language Quirks, Language and Installation. Each feature
  page gets one line saying which pragma turns it on.

## How the compiler does it

Today both switches are one `bool` on the `compiler` (`sane_evaluation_order`, `field_defaults`), set from `main.cpp`.

* **Lexer and parser**: the lexer already turns `;...` into a `COMMENT` token that `parser::load` drops. `load` looks at
  the comment tokens before the first token that is not a comment or a new line, and parses the ones that start with
  `#pragma` into on/off settings. Later feature pragmas produce `pragma-misplaced`.
* **Program settings**: the feature pragmas of the main file, on top of the CLI options, set the existing `bool`s of
  the `compiler` (`sane_evaluation_order`, `field_defaults`) before code generation starts, so the code that reads them
  doesn't change. The feature pragmas of included files are only compared with them, for `pragma-mismatch`.
* **Warnings**: the parser reads includes in place, in the order of the program, so it can keep one stack of warning
  settings for the whole read and record, per file, the settings that start at each line where they change (at the
  first line of an included file too). `compiler::warn` already gets the location of every warning, so it looks up the
  settings in force at that line of that file instead of the ones of the build. The warnings of the parser do the same.
* **Tests**: a CLI test per feature with a main file and an included file in the four combinations (pragma in neither,
  main only, include only, both; only the main file switches, a mismatch warns), plus the precedence of CLI options and
  `no-` forms, the new warnings, and `W` pragmas in a main file and an
  included file (settings flow into an include and back out of it, `push`/`pop` around an `Include`, `Wno-error=` against a
  `-Werror` build), and `push`/`pop` around a block.

Planned PRs, in this order:

1. Pragma parsing, the new warnings, program settings from the main file with `sane-evaluation-order` and
   `field-defaults` as the first two features, `pragma-mismatch`, `--modern` and the `--no-` options.
2. Warning pragmas: positional warning settings with `push`/`pop`.
3. blitz-lsp support.
4. Wiki page.

## Before and after

Today, the build decides:

```blitzbasic
; Gives 3 1 2 with blitzcc game.bb (like the original), and 1 2 3 with blitzcc --sane-evaluation-order game.bb.
Global n = 0
Function NextN()
	n = n + 1
	Return n
End Function
Function Show(a, b, c)
	Print a + " " + b + " " + c
End Function
Show NextN(), NextN(), NextN()
```

With this design, the file decides:

```blitzbasic
;#pragma modern
; Gives 1 2 3 with blitzcc game.bb, whatever options the build adds.
; The original Blitz3D reads the line above as a comment and gives 3 1 2, as before.
Global n = 0
Function NextN()
	n = n + 1
	Return n
End Function
Function Show(a, b, c)
	Print a + " " + b + " " + c
End Function
Show NextN(), NextN(), NextN()
```

## Open questions

1. ~~**Scope**~~: decided by Xaymar (26 Nov 2026): the main file decides for the whole program, feature pragmas in
   included files only warn on a mismatch (`pragma-mismatch`). (Per file was chosen first and dropped the same day.)
2. ~~**Syntax**~~: `;#` as the prefix of all directives, `;#pragma` the first one (Xaymar was fine with `;@` or `;#`,
   26 Nov 2026).
3. ~~**A growing `modern`**~~: decided by Xaymar (26 Nov 2026): `modern` always means the newest set, with a pragma
   per feature (and per warning) to turn single things on or off. No editions.
4. **`--ignore-pragmas`**: wanted now, later, or not at all?
5. ~~**Placement**~~: decided by Xaymar (26 Nov 2026): pragmas that change how the program is compiled must come
   before the first real statement; warning and error pragmas can be anywhere.
6. ~~**Warnings and Include**~~: decided by Xaymar (26 Nov 2026): like in C, warning settings carry into and out of
   `Include`d files; `push`/`pop` keeps them local.
